title: Judgment Operators: A Composition-Invariant Substrate for Multi-Agent Action Spaces
one_liner: Insert a portable decision-time layer that can allow, edit, escalate, or deny agent actions under explicit constraints, so policy violations stop growing with the number of agents in the system.
lead: When many language-model agents are composed together, safety rules and capability rules often fragment across the system. One agent follows one rule, another agent follows another, and violations accumulate as the composition grows. This paper proposes Judgment Operators, a portable intervention layer that sits at action time and can allow, edit, escalate, or deny each action under programmatically checkable constraints, because placing one shared gate at the action boundary stops governance from being split across many agent internals.

problem.h2: Why multi-agent safety degrades as more agents are composed
paras: A single agent can be wrapped with a checker, but a heterogeneous multi-agent system is harder. Different agents may use different prompts, different model families, and different local correction tricks. As these parts are composed, governance becomes fragmented. One unsafe action slipping through one branch can be enough to create a system-level failure.

Local self-correction is not enough because it depends on each agent to notice and repair its own mistakes. Simple blocking filters are also limited because they often reduce task utility by rejecting useful actions without proposing a repair. The paper's premise is that action governance should be centralized at the decision boundary, because then the same explicit constraint logic applies no matter how many agents are upstream.

callout.html: Place a portable judgment layer between every agent and the outside world, and let that layer allow, revise, escalate, or deny actions according to explicit verifiable constraints, because one shared decision point keeps the same rule set active across every branch.

panels.title: 1. Many agents, many rules
panels.viz_args: agent A | agent B | agent C
panels.caption: Governance fragments when each agent handles safety locally.

panels.title: 2. Violations accumulate
panels.caption: More composed agents usually means more ways to fail.

panels.title: 3. Insert judgment operator
panels.caption: Every outbound action passes through the same intervention layer.

panels.title: 4. Repair when possible
panels.caption: The layer preserves utility by editing or escalating when a full denial is unnecessary.

panels.title: 5. Violations stop growing
panels.viz_args: shared enforcement across the composed system
panels.caption: Explicit constraints apply no matter which agent proposed the action.

steps.text: The system writes verifiable rules describing which actions are allowed and which conditions require intervention.
Each agent sends its proposed action to the judgment layer before the action reaches the environment.
The layer either permits the action, revises it into a safe alternative, escalates it for stronger review, or denies it outright because different failures need different levels of intervention.
Only the mediated action reaches the outside world, so all composed agents share the same enforcement surface.
Because the constraint artifact is portable, it can be transferred across models and system compositions without rewriting every agent's internals.

paras: The paper changes where governance lives. It does not ask each agent to internalize every rule. Instead, it moves enforcement to a shared action-time substrate that sits outside the agents. That substrate carries a portable constraint artifact and applies the same intervention semantics everywhere.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: system-level violation probability
hidden.name: System-level violation probability
paras: The hidden quantity is the chance that a composed multi-agent system emits at least one violating action during a task. Without shared mediation, that chance usually rises with the number of agents or branches, because each added component creates another opportunity for a local rule failure.

Judgment Operators are designed to keep this quantity roughly constant with system composition, as long as the explicit constraint layer mediates all relevant actions. That is why composition invariance matters: it says the risk should depend primarily on the quality of the shared mediator, not linearly on how many agent components happened to be assembled upstream.

heat.caption: The paper's target is the growth of system-level violation chance as composition size increases.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the chance that the overall multi-agent system violates a rule at least once during a task.

The framework aims for composition-invariant enforcement by mediating actions through a portable constraint artifact whose intervention semantics do not depend on which upstream agent proposed the action.

paras: The core reason is centralization at the decision boundary. If every proposed action must pass through the same explicit constraint logic, then governance no longer depends on each agent remembering the rule internally. That removes the usual failure pattern where one branch of a composed system lacks the latest safety instruction or interprets it differently.

The four intervention modes preserve utility better than a pure blocking filter because they separate harmless actions from repairable ones. Permit keeps harmless actions moving. Revise repairs actions that are close to acceptable, which saves useful work because the system does not need to throw the entire step away. Escalation reserves harder cases for stronger review, and denial blocks actions that cannot be safely repaired. Together these modes lower violation rate while keeping more task progress than a blanket reject policy because only the truly unsafe actions are fully stopped.

stages.s: Action proposed by any upstream agent
Choose permit, revise, escalate, or deny
Shared governance across the full composed system

math.words: System-level violation probability is the chance that at least one proposed action passes through mediation and still violates a constraint during a task.
math.equation: P_violate(task) = probability(at least one mediated action during the task still breaks a constraint)
symbols: overall chance of a rule violation during one complete task
an action after the judgment layer has allowed, edited, escalated, or denied it
a programmatically checkable rule on permitted behavior
long-run fraction of tasks in which the event occurs

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a task contains 20 proposed actions from several agents.
Without shared mediation, 3 of those actions on average violate a rule somewhere in the workflow, so many runs fail.
With a judgment layer, 15 actions are allowed, 3 are edited, 1 is escalated, and 1 is denied.
If none of the allowed or edited actions violate the constraint after mediation, the task violation count becomes 0.
Across many runs, P_violate(task) is then the fraction of runs where a violating action still slips through after this mediation.

math.note: The important quantity is task-level failure, because one leaked violating action can be enough to compromise the whole run.

charts.title: Local self-correction or pure blocking
charts.note: Local correction misses too many failures, while pure blocking throws away too much useful work.

charts.title: Judgment Operators
charts.note: Shared mediation controls violations and preserves more useful work because edit and escalate are available between allow and deny.

items.html: If important unsafe behaviors are not expressed in the explicit rules, the judgment layer cannot stop them because it only mediates what the constraint set actually describes.
Composition invariance depends on comprehensive coverage. If one branch can act without passing through the operator, system-level violation chance rises again because governance is fragmented.
An edit that changes the action without preserving its intent can damage task utility, so the repair policy must change only what is needed to satisfy the constraint.
Route every relevant action through the operator, define broad enough constraints to cover real risks, and keep edits minimal so the mediated action remains useful while satisfying the rule.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small multi-agent tool-using workflow where several agents can issue file or web actions. Compare three versions: local self-correction, pure blocking filter, and a judgment operator with permit-revise-escalate-deny mediation. Increase the number of agents and branches, then measure how often each system violates explicit action rules and how much task success it retains.
demo.metric_eq: violation_rate = violating_tasks / total_tasks; retained_utility = task_success_with_governance / task_success_without_governance
demo.closing: The demo should show that shared mediation keeps violation rate low as the composition grows because every branch is governed by the same explicit action-time rules.
